title: Is The Sony RX1R III The Perfect Camera For Live Events?
summary: Small, light and less intimidating – Jeremy Cohen shares why the Sony RX1R III helps him take better photos at live events.
body_markdown:
For event photographers, the best camera is often the one that makes it easier to stay present in the room. It needs to be capable enough to keep up with fast-moving moments, comfortable enough to carry throughout a long day, and discreet enough to help people forget they are being photographed.


****


For


[Alpha Collective member Jeremy Cohen](https://alphauniverse.com/member/#/jeremy-cohen) , the


[Sony RX1R III](https://electronics.sony.com/imaging/compact-cameras/all-vlog-compact-cameras/p/dscrx1rm3b?utm_source=AlphaUniverse&utm_medium=Web&utm_campaign=Article) checks those boxes.


****


Photograph by Jeremy Cohen. RX1R III. 1/250-sec. f/11. ISO 640.


Cohen photographs live events with an approach built around movement, proximity and candid connection. He often works one-handed, holding a flash in one hand and the camera in the other – an efficient setup that lets him react quickly as moments unfold.


****


That connection starts with the camera’s small, lightweight form factor. Long event days can mean hours on your feet, constant repositioning and very little downtime. A camera that is easy to handle can make a real difference, especially for photographers who rely on a nimble flash-and-camera workflow.


Photograph by Jeremy Cohen. RX1R III. 1/160-sec. f/11. ISO 1250.


Photograph by Jeremy Cohen. RX1R III. 1/200-sec. f/10. ISO 2000.


“To put it simply, a big reason is because of how small and light the camera is,” Cohen explains. “When I’m shooting, I shoot a lot with one hand, actually. I have a flash in one hand – which is how I like to shoot – and the camera in the other. With the


[Sony RX1R III](https://electronics.sony.com/imaging/compact-cameras/all-vlog-compact-cameras/p/dscrx1rm3b?utm_source=AlphaUniverse&utm_medium=Web&utm_campaign=Article) , this camera is so small and light, I could hold it for a full day and I won’t feel any pain.”


****


Photograph by Jeremy Cohen. RX1R III. 1/160-sec. f/11. ISO 640.


Photograph by Jeremy Cohen. RX1R III. 1/100-sec. f/11. ISO 1000.


That reduced physical burden is not just about comfort. It can help event photographers stay responsive from the first arrival photo through the final dance-floor frame. When the gear feels natural in hand, there is less friction between seeing a moment and capturing it.


****


#### A Less Intimidating Way To Photograph People


The other advantage Cohen sees is more subtle, but just as important:


a smaller camera can change how subjects respond.


****


Professional event setups are often designed to be powerful and dependable, but larger bodies and lenses can sometimes create a barrier between photographer and subject. For candid work, being able to move through a room with a more understated camera can help preserve the feeling of the moment.


****


Photograph by Jeremy Cohen. RX1R III. 1/1250-sec. f/2. ISO 125.


For Cohen, the RX1R III offers a different kind of event-photography experience – one that allows him to work close to the action without overwhelming it. “I feel like it’s not an intimidating camera,” Cohen says. “Having a smaller camera and just photographing people in the moment – candid moments – while just minimizing the gear, I find that it turns out to make for better photos.”


****


#### Designed For Staying In The Moment


****


At live events, the most meaningful photographs are often the ones that don’t have that staged look – a laugh between friends, a quick embrace, a performer’s expression or even a guest fully immersed in the energy of the room. It’s those moments in between the moments, and you need to be nimble and ready to capture them.


****


Photograph by Jeremy Cohen. RX1R III. 1/200-sec. f/10. ISO 2000.


The


[Sony RX1R III’s](https://electronics.sony.com/imaging/compact-cameras/all-vlog-compact-cameras/p/dscrx1rm3b?utm_source=AlphaUniverse&utm_medium=Web&utm_campaign=Article) compact design supports that kind of observation-first approach. It is a camera that can stay out of the way while still giving photographers the confidence to work quickly and intentionally. For event photographers like Cohen, that means less time managing gear and more time watching for the moments that matter.


****


As Cohen’s experience shows, a camera does not need to dominate the room to make powerful images. Sometimes, the smaller setup is exactly what helps the photographer – and the people in front of the lens – feel more at ease.
